subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after collapsing at a party. He is agitated and diaphoretic, with a temperature of 38.1°C, blood pressure 168/102 mm Hg, pulse 118/min, and dilated pupils. He reports intense mid-sternal chest pressure. ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST-segment elevation, and serial troponins are mildly elevated. A urine toxicology screen is positive for cocaine metabolites.
question: What is the most likely mechanism of this patient's chest pain?

options.text: Thrombotic occlusion of a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque
Aortic dissection extending into the coronary ostia
Coronary vasospasm
Prostaglandin-mediated coronary artery inflammation
Coronary microembolization from an infected heart valve

explanation_correct: Cocaine is a classic cause of coronary vasospasm, which presents with chest pain and even myocardial infarction in young patients with otherwise normal coronary arteries. It belongs to the mnemonic CASE for agents causing coronary vasospasm: Cocaine, Amphetamines, Sumatriptan, and Ergot alkaloids. These drugs provoke intense vasospasm of the coronary arteries rather than fixed obstructive lesions.

explanation_incorrect.A: Plaque rupture with thrombosis is the usual mechanism of MI in older patients with coronary risk factors; in cocaine users with normal coronaries, vasospasm is the classic culprit.
explanation_incorrect.B: Aortic dissection can cause chest pain radiating to the back and can occlude a coronary ostium, but this patient has no tearing pain or widened mediastinum, and his tox screen points to cocaine vasospasm.
explanation_incorrect.D: Coronary vasculitis from prostaglandin-mediated inflammation is not a recognized adverse effect of cocaine or amphetamines; the acute mechanism is vasoconstriction, not inflammation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Coronary emboli occur with infective endocarditis or atrial fibrillation; this patient has no murmur, fever with erratic temperature curve, or arrhythmia to suggest a embolic source.

educationalObjective: Coronary vasospasm is caused by Cocaine, Amphetamines, Sumatriptan, and Ergot alkaloids (CASE).

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 62-year-old woman with MRSA bacteremia is receiving IV vancomycin. Thirty minutes into the infusion she develops diffuse pruritic erythema of her face, neck, and upper chest. She is hemodynamically stable with normal blood pressure and no wheezing or angioedema. The infusion is discontinued and her symptoms resolve completely within an hour.
question: What is the most appropriate management to allow her to complete her vancomycin course?

options.text: Resume vancomycin at a slower infusion rate and premedicate with diphenhydramine
Administer intramuscular epinephrine and permanently stop vancomycin
Resume the vancomycin infusion at a faster rate with intravenous fluids
Administer a corticosteroid pulse and desensitize to vancomycin over several days
Obtain serum tryptase and skin-prick testing before any further vancomycin dosing

explanation_correct: This is the vancomycin infusion reaction (formerly called red man syndrome), which results from direct histamine release causing widespread pruritic erythema, typically of the face, neck, and upper torso. It is infusion rate–dependent and is not a true IgE-mediated allergy, so the reaction is managed by slowing the infusion rate and giving an antihistamine such as diphenhydramine, allowing the drug to be continued.

explanation_incorrect.B: Epinephrine is reserved for anaphylaxis with hypotension, airway compromise, or bronchospasm. This hemodynamically stable, self-limited flushing reaction does not require discontinuing the drug.
explanation_incorrect.C: A faster infusion would worsen the reaction, since flushing is directly related to the rate of vancomycin infusion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Corticosteroids and multi-day desensitization are measures for true hypersensitivity reactions; the infusion reaction is due to histamine release and needs only rate reduction and antihistamine.
explanation_incorrect.E: Allergy workup with tryptase and skin testing is unnecessary because this is not an IgE-mediated allergic reaction; it is a predictable, rate-dependent pharmacologic effect.

educationalObjective: The vancomycin infusion reaction (red man syndrome) is infusion rate–dependent histamine release managed with a slower infusion and diphenhydramine.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 55-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer develops progressive exertional dyspnea and bilateral ankle swelling. An echocardiogram shows biventricular dilation with an LVEF of 28%, reduced from 60% at baseline six months ago. Coronary angiography shows no obstructive disease. She has received a multidrug chemotherapy regimen over the past year.
question: Which of the following chemotherapy agents is the most likely cause of her cardiac findings?

options.text: Cyclophosphamide
Paclitaxel
Trastuzumab
5-Fluorouracil
Doxorubicin

explanation_correct: Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin and daunorubicin are classic causes of dilated cardiomyopathy with dose-dependent reduction in LVEF, which may be prevented with the iron-chelating agent dexrazoxane. This patient's new biventricular dilation and severely depressed ejection fraction without coronary disease is the hallmark presentation. Trastuzumab also can cause dilated cardiomyopathy, but the prototypical and most commonly tested causative agent is doxorubicin.

explanation_incorrect.A: Cyclophosphamide is associated with hemorrhagic cystitis and, at high doses, SIADH, but it is not a classic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy.
explanation_incorrect.B: Paclitaxel causes hypersensitivity reactions related to its cremophor vehicle and peripheral neuropathy, not a dilated cardiomyopathy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Trastuzumab can cause reversible cardiomyopathy, but in a question of the single most likely classic cause, anthracyclines such as doxorubicin are the prototypical agents; trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is generally less severe and often reversible.
explanation_incorrect.D: 5-Fluorouracil is classically associated with coronary vasospasm causing chest pain, not with dilated cardiomyopathy.

educationalObjective: Anthracyclines (doxorubicin, daunorubicin) cause dilated cardiomyopathy, which can be prevented with dexrazoxane.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 44-year-old woman with chronic pain syndrome maintained on methadone develops infectious diarrhea and is treated with erythromycin. Five days later she presents after a witnessed syncopal episode. ECG shows a rapid polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QRS complexes that appear to twist around the baseline. Electrolytes are normal except for a serum potassium of 3.2 mEq/L.
question: What is the most likely explanation for her arrhythmia?

options.text: Additive prolongation of the QT interval leading to torsades de pointes
Cocaine- and methadone-mediated coronary vasospasm with ischemia
Erythromycin-induced cholestatic hepatitis causing fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
Histamine release from methadone causing tachyarrhythmia
Atrial fibrillation with aberrant ventricular conduction

explanation_correct: Both methadone and macrolides are QT-prolonging agents, so their combination additively prolongs repolarization and precipitates torsades de pointes, the polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that twists around the baseline. Remember the QT-prolonging ABCDEF: antiArrhythmics (class IA, III), antiBiotics (macrolides, fluoroquinolones), anti'C'ychotics (eg, ziprasidone), antiDepressants (TCAs), antiEmetics (ondansetron), and antiFungals (fluconazole), as well as methadone. Her mild hypokalemia further increases risk.

explanation_incorrect.B: Methadone is not one of the CASE agents for coronary vasospasm, and the described arrhythmia — polymorphic VT twisting around the baseline — is torsades de pointes, not ischemia-driven monomorphic VT.
explanation_incorrect.C: Erythromycin can cause acute cholestatic hepatitis and jaundice, but that would present with jaundice and RUQ symptoms and does not produce a prolonged QT interval or torsades.
explanation_incorrect.D: Histamine release is the mechanism of the vancomycin infusion reaction, not a property of methadone, and histamine release does not cause torsades de pointes.
explanation_incorrect.E: Atrial fibrillation with aberrancy produces an irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia, whereas this ECG shows a rapid polymorphic ventricular rhythm characteristic of torsades.

educationalObjective: QT-prolonging agents (ABCDEF plus methadone) cause torsades de pointes, and combining two such agents markedly increases risk.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 66-year-old man with hypertension is started on amlodipine. At a follow-up visit six weeks later his blood pressure is well controlled at 126/78 mm Hg, but he reports progressive bilateral ankle swelling that is worse at the end of the day and improves overnight. He has no dyspnea, orthopnea, or unilateral leg swelling. Cardiac and lung exams are normal, and his kidneys are functioning normally.
question: What is the most likely mechanism of his leg swelling?

options.text: Development of heart failure from negative inotropic effects
Mineralocorticoid-mediated renal sodium retention
Deep venous thrombosis of both legs
Arteriolar dilation increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure
Glomerular protein loss reducing plasma oncotic pressure

explanation_correct: Peripheral edema is the classic adverse effect of dihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers such as amlodipine. Selective arteriolar (precapillary) dilation raises hydrostatic pressure in the capillary beds of the lower extremities, driving fluid into the interstitium. The edema is bilateral, dependent, and not accompanied by signs of heart failure, and it improves with leg elevation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Dihydropyridine CCBs have minimal negative inotropic effect and do not cause decompensated heart failure; the patient has no dyspnea, elevated JVP, rales, or S3.
explanation_incorrect.B: Sodium retention via mineralocorticoid activity is not a property of amlodipine; drugs causing sodium and water retention would produce generalized edema rather than purely dependent ankle swelling.
explanation_incorrect.C: Unilateral leg swelling with calf tenderness would suggest DVT, but this patient has bilateral, symmetric, dependent edema with normal exams, which is the typical pattern of drug-induced vasodilatory edema.
explanation_incorrect.E: Proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia cause periorbital and generalized edema, not isolated dependent ankle swelling, and his renal function is normal.

educationalObjective: Dihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers (eg, amlodipine) cause peripheral edema via precapillary arteriolar dilation.
